After one cycle of pembrolizumab, the symptoms improved, and chest radiography showed remarkable remission.</p><p id="Par8931">
<bold>Conclusion:</bold> To our knowledge, this is the first report eliciting the presence of intratumoral lymphocytes within the pulmonary tissues at the maximal timing of pseudoprogression. Our current case suggested that progressive exacerbation within 4 weeks from the initiation of anti-PD-1 antibody displays the possibility of pseudoprogression, and the radiographic entity of pulmonary exacerbation could be explained by the presence of TILs.</p><p id="Par8932">Funding: Tomonori Kawasaki is supported by Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research (No. 21K06910 and No. 20K08131) from the Japanese Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology and the National Hospital Organization (NHO) Grant (H29-NHO-01).</p><p id="Par8933">

<bold>Atypical spindle cell lipomatous tumour: a rare case report</bold>
</p><p id="Par9155">
<underline>J. Baena-Del Valle*</underline>, D.M. Bertel-Rodriguez, M.A. Palau-Lazaro</p><p id="Par9156">*Fundacion Santa Fe De Bogota, Universidad De Los Andes, Colombia</p><p id="Par9157">
<bold>Background &amp; objectives:</bold> Atypical Spindle Cell / Pleomorphic Lipomatous Tumour (ASCLT) are recently described neoplasms, characterized by lipoma-like appearance but with atypical and spindle cell histological features. They resemble pleomorphic lipoma, but are larger in size and with a broader anatomic distribution.</p><p id="Par9158">
<bold>Methods:</bold> We present a 34-year-old woman with a 10 x 8 x 3 cm mass in the right knee. A biopsy reported a lipomatous lesion and a resection was performed. Microscopy showed a lipomatous neoplasm with predominantly well-differentiated adipocytic component, and a smaller proportion of lipoblasts and pleomorphic cells in a fibrous matrix. No necrosis and mitosis were identified.</p><p id="Par9159">
<bold>Results:</bold> Tumour cells were positive for CD34 and S100, and negative for MDM2 and CDK4. The case was sent for consultation to Dr Christopher Fletcher, supporting the diagnosis of ASCLT. No recurrence has been reported so far.</p><p id="Par9160">ASCLT mostly occur in middle-aged adults with a slight male preference and a variable size (up to 28 cm). They have an indolent behaviour with no or very low rate of local recurrence, and no risk for dedifferentiation or metastasis.</p><p id="Par9161">
<bold>Conclusion:</bold> It is crucial to differentiate ASCLT from other lipomatous lesions such as atypical lipomatous tumour/well-differentiated liposarcoma, pleomorphic liposarcoma and low-grade dedifferentiated liposarcoma, due to their frequent recurrence and capacity to metastasize. Immunohistochemistry helps in this situation, since even though weak and focal expression of MDM2 and CDK4 may be seen, they do not occur in combination. Also, loss of Rb expression is frequently seen (79%).</p><p id="Par9162">

<bold>Background &amp; objectives:</bold> Epithelioid angiosarcoma (EA) is a rare endothelial cell malignancy. The aetiology is unknown and association with implanted foreign bodies is very rare. <bold>Methods:</bold> A 47 year old woman with history of surgery for an ovarian cyst 19 years ago, presented with abdominal pain and constipation for at least 4 days. <bold>Methods:</bold> We present the case of a 22-year-old female, admitted to “Foisor” Orthopedics Hospital for pain in the left knee. <bold>Methods:</bold> A 77 year-old male patient was admitted for scheduled radical cystoprostatectomy due to previously diagnosed muscle invasive (T2) squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder on TURBT chips. Gross examination of the bladder specimen revealed a whitish exophytic friable tumour, measuring 9X4cm, along with areas of ulceration.</p><p id="Par9622">
<bold>Results:</bold> Histopathological examination revealed two distinct and in close proximity malignant cell populations; a squamous cell carcinoma component mostly regarding the exophytic tumour and a high-grade malignant spindle cell tumour infiltrating large portion of the muscle wall and partially invading the pervesical fat. The latter also showed areas of osseous differentiation. In situ urothelial carcinoma was also present in the superficial epithelium. Prostate, bilateral seminal vesicles, vas deferens, and ureteric margins were free of tumour. The aforementioned results established the diagnosis of sarcomatoid carcinoma.</p><p id="Par9623">
<bold>Conclusion:</bold> Bladder sarcomatoid carcinoma is a rare malignant type and is estimated to account for 0.1%–0.3% of all bladder tumours. Less than 100 case reports have been published in the literature. It is characterized by the presence of an epithelial urothelial and a sarcomatous population. For most cases the epithelial component is urothelial carcinoma, however, squamous cell and small cell carcinoma components have also frequently been reported. Due to aggressive nature of disease, it is usually diagnosed at advanced stage.</p><p id="Par9624">

<underline>J. Baena-Del Valle*</underline>, D.M. Bertel-Rodriguez, M. Plata-Salazar, M.A. Palau-Lazaro</p><p id="Par9739">*Fundacion Santa Fe De Bogota, Universidad De Los Andes, Colombia</p><p id="Par9740">
<bold>Background &amp; objectives:</bold> Solitary Fibrous Tumour (SFT) of the prostate is rare, with approximately 50 cases reported, 14 confirmed after the discovery of the NAD2-STAT6 fusion. We present a case of a middle-age-adult with a SFT presenting as an Intravesical Prostatic Protrusion (IPP).</p><p id="Par9741">
<bold>Methods:</bold> A 42-year-old man with a 5-year history of urinary retention and suprapubic pain, was diagnosed with a benign prostatic hyperplasia, and treated with alpha-blockers. One year later he had persistence of the symptoms and an ultrasound revealed an enlarged prostate with a lesion protruding into the urinary bladder lumen (17 mm). A transurethral resection of the prostate was performed.</p><p id="Par9742">
<bold>Results:</bold> Microscopic examination showed a mesenchymal neoplasm with variably cellular patternless pattern, cells were spindled to ovoid with uniform nuclei, branching staghorn vessels, and areas of fibrosis, without necrosis. 7 mitosis per mm2 were identified. Neoplastic cells were diffusely positive for STAT6 and CD34, and Ki-67 rate was 7%. A diagnosis of intermediate-risk SFT was made. Patient is currently being followed up with no evidence of recurrence or metastasis.</p><p id="Par9743">Prostate-SFT mean age of presentation is 55 years, and most patients present with obstructive urinary symptoms. Presenting as an IPP is extremely unusual. Morphologic features are similar to extraprostatic SFTs and most of them are positive for STAT6, CD34, Bcl-2 and CD99.</p><p id="Par9744">
<bold>Conclusion:</bold> Many metastatic risk models have been developed; the most widely used, also validated in extra thoracic SFTs, includes mitosis, patient age, and tumour size to classify tumours into low, intermediate, and high risk. Recurrence and metastasis are rare. Complete surgical resection is the treatment of choice and the most important prognostic factor. Chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy should be considered as palliative treatment.</p><p id="Par9745">

<bold>Background &amp; objectives:</bold> Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) accounts for 2% of all new cancer cases in adults. Although spontaneous regression in primary RCC and metastases is rare, it is a well-known phenomenon.</p><p id="Par9750">
<bold>Methods:</bold> We report two cases of spontaneous regression of RCC in an 81-year-old and a 70-year-old male that underwent partial nephrectomy for an incidental kidney mass. The entire lesion was sampled in both cases, and immunohistochemistry studies were performed.</p><p id="Par9751">
<bold>Results:</bold> In the first case, a 4.5 cm haemorrhagic and necrotic mass separated from the parenchyma by a smooth thick fibrous capsule was observed macroscopically. <sup><bold>TM</bold></sup>
<bold>Precision Assay on the Genexus</bold><sup><bold>TM</bold></sup>
<bold>System for accurate identification of cancer biomarkers in FFPE and liquid biopsy samples</bold></p><p id="Par9949">
<underline>J. Schageman*</underline>, T. Jayaweera, N. Siepert, B. Hradecky, E. Ostrowska, I. Casuga, K. Lea, P. Kshatriya, J. Gu, R. Cao, A. Cheng, K. Bramlett</p><p id="Par9950">*Thermo Fisher Scientific, Austin, TX, United States</p><p id="Par9951">

<bold>Methods:</bold> Contrived and clinical research samples with known variants were used for the OPA FFPE and liquid biopsy workflows (n = 30). Extracted NA was transferred to the Genexus<sup>TM</sup> sequencer for library preparation, sequencing, variant and QC reporting using the onboard Ion Torrent™ analysis software.</p><p id="Par9953">

Excess NA was automatically aliquoted into an archive plate and stored for future use. Sequencing results for four samples of FFPE or liquid biopsy were reported within 24 hours. Both Control and clinical research samples showed expected assay metrics including read coverage, molecular coverage, and uniformity. Molecular classification was assessed by Polymerase Chain Reaction, based on 22 gene panel proposed by Northcott et al 2012, plus ANO2, DISC1, ARHGAP18, GMR8, PRDM6. The expression of the novel genes was evaluated between the four groups and compared with four cerebellar control samples.</p><p id="Par9970">
<bold>Results:</bold> Using the 22 subgroup signature genes, samples were classified as 8/75 wingless, 27/75 sonic hedgehog, 22/75 group 3, and 18/75 group 4 medulloblastomas.</p><p id="Par9971">Thereafter, when compared between the four subgroups, mean fold change values for ANO2 were 4.00, 1.20, 8.46 and 10.18; for DISC1 were 17.36, 15.22, 12.28 and 19.72; for ARHGAP18 were 2.52, 4.28, 14.71 and 8.59; for GRM8 were 152.9, 814.7, 230.6 and 1381.9; and, for PRDM6 were 16.21, 11.57, 19.26, and 27.40, for wingless, sonic hedgehog, group 3, and group 4, respectively.</p><p id="Par9972">Consequently, the overexpression of ANO2, DISC1, GRM8 and PRDM6 were consistent with group 4, while overexpression of ARHGAP18 with group 3 subgroup assignment.</p><p id="Par9973">
<bold>Conclusion:</bold> This study confirms differential expression of the five genes analysed between the four main molecular subgroups of medulloblastoma, furthermore, help to differentiate amongst groups 3 and 4.</p><p id="Par9974">Outputs provide continued support for group 3 and group 4 distinction. Next step is to validate the set of genes by methylation or with an independent validation cohort of medulloblastomas. Supplementary studies may also provide insights to facilitate groups 3 and 4 subtypification using the evaluated genes.</p><p id="Par9975">Funding: Governmental grants (Fondos Federales México HIM/2018/092).</p></sec></sec><sec id="fn-group1" sec-type="fn-group" disp-level="1"><title>Footnotes</title><fn-group><fn id="fn1"><p><bold>Publisher’s note</bold></p><p>Springer Nature remains neutral with regard to jurisdictional claims in published maps and institutional affiliations.</p></fn><fn id="fn2"><p><bold>Change history</bold></p><p>12/24/2022</p><p>A Correction to this paper has been published: 10.1007/s00428-022-03483-5</p></fn><fn id="fn3"><p><bold>Change history</bold></p><p>10/1/2022</p><p>A Correction to this paper has been published: 10.1007/s00428-022-03419-z</p></fn><fn id="fn4"><p><bold>Change history</bold></p><p>8/26/2022</p><p>A Correction to this paper has been published: 10.1007/s00428-022-03401-9</p></fn><fn id="fn5"><p><bold>Change history</bold></p><p>9/15/2022</p><p>A Correction to this paper has been published: 10.1007/s00428-022-03405-5</p></fn></fn-group></sec></body></article>
